articles.title: On the road with pro-independence Albertans, one small town at a time

image.caption: Chris Scott is with the group Let’s Talk Alberta. Last week, they toured around southern Alberta, handing out lawn signs and talking to residents about independence. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

blocks.text: We hit the road with separatists as they meet supporters in rural Alberta
Chris Scott sat in the driver’s seat of his 2001 Monaco Dynasty motorhome last week, bumping along the network of rural highways in southern Alberta.
The vehicle creaked a bit. Some leather-covered furniture was cracking, and some cabinet drawer latches didn’t work anymore.
It’s like Alberta, Scott said: you can ignore problems and let them get worse, or you can pay attention to them and fix them.
“I see there's a lot of things going on with Alberta that need some care and attention,” said Scott.

The restaurant owner, who gained prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, has hit the road this summer to talk independence, travelling with a group of people who also support the idea of Alberta becoming its own nation.
CBC News recently spent a day aboard the “Let’s Talk Alberta” bus, speaking with passengers about what motivates them at a time when Albertans are weighing their vote in an Oct. 19 referendum.

Earlier this summer, CBC spent time with volunteers helping the pro-Canada group Forever Canadian, talking to them about their efforts and why they wouldn’t be voting to have a future referendum on whether Alberta should stay in the country.

Federalist and separatist groups have been a common sight this summer, fundraising and shaking hands with voters at events like the Calgary Stampede. Voter mobilization efforts are expected to ramp up considerably with less than two months to go to the referendum.
On the bus
On a recent weekday in August, Scott’s bus hit the road for a 10-stop tour through the southern part of the province.
Scott’s passengers included Jasper Smit, a friend from the Netherlands who runs a social media channel called CommonSense TV.
Leaning on a countertop in the back of the motorhome, Smit studied the packaging of a snack purchased from a highway gas station. He read it aloud: roasted grilled pepperoni cheesesteak.
“Mystery meat!” called out another rider.
The wrapping on the bus’ exterior was less ambiguous.

The vehicle is emblazoned with the “Let’s Talk Alberta” decal, framed by provincial viewscapes: the hoodoos of Drumheller flowing into sweeping mountains and rivers, topped by an expansive prairie sky. It was an Alberta postcard, designed with artificial intelligence and then smoothed out by a designer.

On the back of the vehicle, a Bible verse printed in script: Jeremiah 29:7 — "Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile. Pray to the Lord for it, because if it prospers, you too will prosper."
It was Scott who procured the motorhome to criss-cross the province.
With a full standup shower and decent-sized bed in the back, Scott could spend days on the bus if he needed to.
Increasingly, he has been, as he’s travelled to all corners of the province with the clock running down to voting day.
He carries with him his experiences from the pandemic.
He was charged and later acquitted for breaching public health restrictions during COVID-19 related to his Whistle Stop Cafe in east-central Alberta.

Scott was highly critical of politicians that he viewed as allowing laws that "strip our fundamental rights and freedoms away." His reputation has made him something of a folk hero amongst those who share his views in these small towns.
“I just learned that if there's something that's wrong, you need to stand up for yourself,” Scott said of his experience.
When the bus pulls into a town, it’s often greeted with supporters. Some caught word of the trip on social media.
In Rosemary, Alta., with a population of little more than 350, a lone man who came out to get a lawn sign said he heard news of the trip on a Facebook group entitled, “Bassano Bitching or Bragging.”
“The whole thing is really not about separation, in my opinion,” said Bassano resident Tom Schaffer.
“It's about making the government wake up and go, hey, these guys might want to separate. Maybe we should actually do something and listen to them?”

Tanya Clemens, co-leader of a separate Alberta independence group, Let Alberta Decide, was on the bus too, as was John Bolton, a former Calgary radio host who now provides emcee services at various independence events, and Patti Vold, a mother of nine and a grandmother of 15.

There was also Sandy Duguay, who was born and raised in Montreal, where she lived through two referendums as an English speaker. Duguay also spent 26 years in Victoria, where her husband was a chaplain at a prison on Vancouver Island.

Duguay was never involved in politics before, but was motivated to become political after the COVID-19 pandemic hit, which evolved into helping the Alberta independence signature drive. She’s now travelling full-time on the bus.
“I feel very close to these people,” Duguay said, who turns 72 in a few weeks.

As the bus weaved its way along the route, the conversation snaked through the group’s motivating complaints with the federal government. Some, like frustration with the federal equalization program or Ottawa’s approach to firearms, have been kindling for alienation for years.
The cultural divide at play quickly came into focus, too. Certain federal bills, perhaps less familiar to the broader Canadian public, are viewed by this group as threats to religious freedom.

“Bill C-9 especially,” Duguay said, referring to the Combatting Hate Act, which amends the Criminal Code to strengthen penalties for hate crimes. The Liberals received support from the Bloc Québécois after including a clause to remove a religious exemption from the country's hate speech laws.

items: Contentious anti-hate legislation passes final vote in the House, now moves to Senate

blocks.text: The Conservatives have argued that amounts to an “assault” on religious freedoms, while Justice Minister Sean Fraser has said the new law won’t “criminalize faith.”
“Look what’s happened to Europe,” Duguay said, turning to Smit. “You were founded on Judeo-Christian principles. And you guys were the first to get rid of them."

Wearing a Let’s Talk Alberta shirt and a Whistle Stop hat, Smit, the visitor from the Netherlands, didn’t entirely agree. He said he's “not religious at all" and that embedding Christian principles into governance would set a precedent that would require adopting other religious laws whenever demographics shifted in the future.
“In all fairness, you should bring that [into] politics,” he said.
Vold, the grandmother of 15, feels Christian values have been fading from public life, which is pushing society towards moral decline.

“For many, many years, the idea was you shouldn't mix church and state, right? I disagree,” Vold said. “The state should not be in the church, but people of faith should be in the state. They should be helping to guide the country.”
Soon after this conversation, the bus arrived in Strathmore and pulled near Kinsmen Park. Scott and Smit exited. Talk of faith continued, until suddenly, Smit ran back up the bus stairs.
“The police are here.”
A heated confrontation
Outside the bus, a crowd had formed in the parking lot.

Various supporters of the independence movement who had arrived to greet the bus gathered around Scott as he was engaged in an argument. On the other side was a town official, flanked by a peace officer.
“So anyway, we'll be here for about an hour,” Scott said.
“I’m asking you to leave,” the official responded. The group was free to express its opinions, the man said, but not on the town’s property.
“But I can,” Scott responded. “It’s public property.”
The crowd grew increasingly frustrated. Scott was told that if he did not move the vehicle, the RCMP would be called.
“Well, I mean, it’s not the first time I’ve been arrested,” Scott said.
Minutes passed. Separatist influencers began to livestream from the scene. Eventually, word came that the bus was allowed to stay.

“The town respects individuals' right to peacefully express their views and participate in democratic processes,” a town spokesperson later said in an email to CBC News. “The group was able to continue gathering and expressing its views.”
The bus moved on to an Airdrie pizza place that’s become a gathering spot for the separatist movement.

Behind schedule and with three stops still to go, the Let’s Talk Alberta crew sat down and scarfed down slices, with a Toronto Blue Jays game playing on the screens above and curious onlookers surrounding the crowd of blue shirts.
One man asked what the group was doing there.
“It’s an Alberta independence bus tour,” he was told.
The man grimaced.
Polling suggests that support for independence is stronger in the rural regions, and Let’s Talk Alberta’s tour last week to smaller locales was largely met by receptive crowds.
But to win in October, the group understands it needs to make gains in the cities, where it hasn't received as friendly a welcome as it has in rural Alberta. That’s where they're headed next.
“September, October will be all cities,” Duguay said. “The cities, different cultures, different mindsets … we’ve covered just about every little town. But now, the cities.”

articles.title: Go eyes funding for school counselors
articles.summary: Sen. Bong Go said he will closely scrutinize the government’s education budget to ensure that adequate funding is provided for school counselors and mental health personnel, as new Department…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bong Go said he will closely scrutinize the government’s education budget to ensure that adequate funding is provided for school counselors and mental health personnel, as new Department of Education (DepEd) data showed that fewer than 1,000 registered guidance counselors are serving more than 45,000 schools nationwide.

The senator, who chairs the Senate committees on youth and sports, said the shortage deserves particular attention during congressional deliberations on the national budget, especially amid recent incidents of school violence, bullying and other concerns affecting the well-being of Filipino learners.
Go said the government must make sure these created positions are actually funded, filled, deployed and sustained so students can access mental health and psychosocial support when they need it.
“Mental health issue is real. This is real,” Go stressed during the Senate hearing on the recent school shooting in Zamboanga City.

DepEd Undersecretary Willie Cabral disclosed that while around 5,000 registered guidance counselors were recorded nationwide as of Jan. 31, fewer than 1,000 were actually serving under the agency. These personnel have to respond to the needs of learners spread across more than 45,000 schools.

The department had created around 5,000 guidance counselor positions in 2020, but only about 1,000 of these were eventually filled, underscoring the difficulty of translating authorized positions into personnel actually working in schools.

articles.title: Palace defends President Marco’s singing at First Lady Liza Marco’s birthday
articles.summary: President Marcos has drawn flak over online videos showing him singing during the birthday celebration of First Lady Liza Marcos while some areas were inundated by floods caused by the southwest…

blocks.text: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos meet the Filipino community in Melbourne, Australia on March 4, 2024.
PPA pool photos by Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has drawn flak over online videos showing him singing during the birthday celebration of First Lady Liza Marcos while some areas were inundated by floods caused by the southwest monsoon.
A backdrop of the stage where Marcos delivered song numbers showed that the event took place on Aug. 26 and carried the theme “Liza and the Chocolate Factory.”
The First Lady turned 67 on Aug. 21.
Palace press officer Claire Castro, however, said the government’s operations did not stop even if the President spent some time with his family.

“The President is the President wherever he is. His spending of some time with his family did not mean that the performance of his mandate or the operations of the government stopped,” Castro said in a text message.

In one of the videos, the President was seen belting out “You,” a ballad popularized by Filipino music icon Basil Valdez. In another video, Marcos was shown singing “And I Love Her” by British pop band The Beatles.
The videos were posted online by Vigan City Mayor Jose Singson Jr. on Aug. 28 and have since been reposted by various news organizations and social media users.

Marcos’ critics have accused him of being insensitive, saying he was partying while people in flooded areas were suffering. Some social media users have also questioned the President’s quality of leadership, claiming he was out of touch with the experiences of ordinary Filipinos, especially those in flood-hit areas.
Castro also responded to former presidential spokesman Harry Roque’s statement that the President was having a concert while Pampanga and Bulacan were submerged in floods.

“Let us not forget that the President prioritized the site visits and inspections in Pampanga and Bulacan to improve the plight of our countrymen and to deliver assistance to the affected. Members of the media witnessed this last Monday,” she said.

“The little time and one night the President spent with his wife, his family and other people close to him to thank God for the gift of life given to his spouse does not mean he abandoned his obligation to the nation. It did not happen during the height of the cyclone last Friday or Saturday,” she said.
Castro reiterated that the President remains focused and has asked agencies to act swiftly on the effect of the monsoon rains.
“In conditions like this, he chose to remain in the Philippines to continue his monitoring,” the Palace press officer added.
About eight million people in 10 regions have been affected by the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng, according to latest government data.

articles.title: DPWH, PRA halt reclamation in Taguig
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways and the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) have issued a cease-and-desist order against an unauthorized reclamation project along the Taguig…

blocks.text: Department of Public Works and Highways.
Businessworld / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Public Works and Highways and the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) have issued a cease-and-desist order against an unauthorized reclamation project along the Taguig waterfront, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said yesterday.

Speaking during a field inspection in Marikina, Dizon confirmed that the formal order was executed following explicit directives from the Office of the President to halt illegal earth-filling and coastal development activities along Laguna de Bay.
Dizon said the order was served on Aug. 20 and took effect immediately.

The PRA, an attached agency under the Office of the President, oversees all reclamation civil works nationwide. Unsanctioned projects have come under intense scrutiny from public works and environmental officials for disrupting natural drainage channels and compounding severe monsoon flooding across Metro Manila and surrounding river basins.
Dizon said that multi-agency coordination meetings have been convened to resolve jurisdiction, environmental impact and legal violations surrounding the project.

“A meeting has been called with key stakeholders, including the city government of Taguig, the Laguna Lake Development Authority and the Pasig River Urban Development Project,” he said. “We will discuss the issues and determine the way forward, but all reclamation activities are ordered stopped effective immediately.”

The DPWH chief emphasized that the government will strictly enforce coastal and riverbank regulations to ensure development projects do not compromise Metro Manila’s overall flood control master plan.

articles.title: Tour for Asean leaders’ spouses set
articles.summary: Filipino traditional arts, fashion, entertainment and food are expected to gain the spotlight during the tour of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders’ spouses at the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Filipino traditional arts, fashion, entertainment and food are expected to gain the spotlight during the tour of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders’ spouses at the Likhang Filipino in Pasay City this November.
First Lady Liza Marcos provided details of the tour after a meeting with the National Organizing Council (NOC) and representatives of ASEAN countries last Aug. 28.

“Productive briefing with the NOC and the other ASEAN country representatives during their walk through for the upcoming Spouses’ Tour at Likhang Filipino,” the First Lady posted on Facebook yesterday.
“Thrilled to hear their positive feedback on our detailed preparations – and even more excited to welcome our ASEAN First Ladies this November!”
The planned activities include the witnessing of a float parade with marching bands, the performance of folk dances from Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao and a fashion show.

articles.title: Local hog producers sound alarm over gov’t swine repopulation delays
articles.summary: The Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines Inc. (ProPork) expects government efforts to restore the country’s pig population to pre-African Swine Fever (ASF) levels to bear fruit by 2030,…

blocks.text: The Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines Inc. (ProPork) expects government efforts to restore the country’s pig population to pre-African Swine Fever (ASF) levels to bear fruit by 2030, rather than 2028.

“At the rate of implementation for the government’s repopulation programs, which have been delayed, they will only accomplish their objective of restoring the population by 2030,” said ProPork President Erik Harina in an interview last week.
The Department of Agriculture (DA) aims to bring the domestic hog inventory back to around 13 million heads by 2028 through initiatives designed to boost productivity.

Under its ₱1.6-billion swine repopulation program, the DA plans to procure around 32,000 gilts, or young female pigs that have not yet given birth, to distribute to multiplier farms for breeding and piglet redistribution.
“No pigs have been purchased or delivered to recipients yet, and it is already September, with the year nearing its end,” Harina noted.
He added that even if the DA rolls out the program early next year, the country’s hog population will likely only reach pre-ASF levels by 2030.
Based on preliminary data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), total hog inventory fell to 8.93 million heads by the end of June from 9.01 million heads a year ago.
Smallholder farms accounted for the bulk of the herd at 7.08 million heads, followed by commercial farms with 1.7 million heads and semi-commercial farms with 149,216 heads.
To ensure sustained recovery in hog supply, Harina said the government must complement its repopulation push with aggressive vaccination drives, as the threat of ASF persists.
Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) data showed that as of Aug. 7, active ASF cases were still present across 60 barangays in 41 municipalities across 20 provinces.

Additionally, ProPork is pressing the government to restore original tariff rates under the minimum access volume (MAV) system for pork imports. Currently, imported pork within the 204,210-metric ton (MT) quota carries a 15-percent tariff, while out-of-quota shipments are taxed at 25 percent. ProPork wants to raise these rates to 30 percent and 40 percent, respectively.

Harina argued that higher tariffs would curb the inflow of cheaper pork imports, giving local hog raisers stronger incentive to expand production. He noted that higher duties would also generate additional revenue for the Animal Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (AnCEF), which helps finance the DA’s repopulation programs.
For now, the country remains heavily reliant on foreign pork to plug the supply deficit.
According to the BAI, the Philippines imported 541,405 MT of pork products from January to July, a 10 percent increase from the 490,825 MT brought in over the same period last year.

articles.title: PSEi to bounce at week' start, take cues from inflation towards Friday
articles.summary: The local stock market may start the week with some bargain-hunting, after the PSEi suffered its steepest weekly drop of the year last week, although investors will be positioning later in the week,…

blocks.text: The local stock market may start the week with some bargain-hunting, after the PSEi suffered its steepest weekly drop of the year last week, although investors will be positioning later in the week, ahead of the release of the August inflation numbers on Friday.

“Next week, we may see a technical bounce driven by bargain hunting. The medium-term outlook is still bearish, however, given the weakening economic outlook,” said Philstocks Financial Research Manager Japhet Tantiangco.

He noted that, “At its closing last week, the local market stood at a price-to-earnings ratio of 10.6 times, below the last five years’ average of 14.4 times and the regional average of 16.2 times. This implies that the bourse is at bargain levels setting it up for a possible bounce in the short run.”

Sentiment-wise, Tantiangco said the weakness of the Peso may discourage foreign investors from getting into the Philippine equity market. Economy-wise, while a weak Peso may benefit exporters and OFWs, it is also expected to raise import costs which, in turn, is an upside risk to inflation.

He added that, technical charts are also showing the possibility of a brief rebound before another round of bearish moves, thus, “Taking all of these into consideration, investors are advised to remain cautious.”

For its part, online brokerage 2TradeAsia.com said the Bangko Sentral trimmed its 2026 average inflation forecast to 6.1 percent (from 6.4 percent), on softer recent data and lower oil, but lifted the 2027 number to 5.4 percent (from 4.5 percent), with a return toward the three percent target only expected in 2028.

“Working backward, hitting the 2026 full-year number implies August to December needs to average somewhere around five to 5.5 percent, which points to some easing from hereon. Given a fairly high year-ago base, the working estimate is around 6.2 percent,” it noted.

However, 2TradeAsia.com said that the risk is skewed to the upside in August, as the same weather disruption the BSP cited last Thursday hits food and transport right as harvest timing gets scrambled, so a print north of six percent would not surprise and keep the hawkish tilt intact into the fourth quarter.

Meanwhile, it noted that macro headwinds are compounding chart weakness; for instance, Moody's sharp GDP revision to three percent (down from four percent) pressures a broad mark down of earnings growth targets across the index.

Also, renewed interest in AI and semicon plays abroad are likely to keep foreign hands absent, so “a meaningful market bounce hinges on domestic institutional funds stepping in to absorb foreign supply, yet conviction remains thin without fundamental catalyst support.”

Heading into the final third of the year, with several stocks at historic lows, the brokerage said to “expect gradual positioning. Balance portfolio selection with defensives, and possibly select metals & commodities shares.”
For stock picks, RCBC Securities has a BUY rating for Maynilad Water Services, Inc. due to the firm’s robust operational execution and disciplined cost control.
It noted that Maynilad continues to execute its key operational initiatives to mitigate El Niño risks and lessen its reliance on Angat Dam.

“These proactive measures proved effective when Angat Dam reached a record low of 150.60meters on July 25, 2026, as Maynilad sustained continuous water service across its concession without initiating service interruptions, the brokerage said.

articles.title: BSP moves to mandate emergency credit lines for top lenders
articles.summary: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is proposing new rules to compel domestic systemically important banks to maintain emergency credit lines and submit to annual access testing to bolster…

blocks.text: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is proposing new rules to compel domestic systemically important banks to maintain emergency credit lines and submit to annual access testing to bolster operational readiness in the country’s financial sector.

According to a draft circular amending the Manual of Regulations for Banks, the central bank seeks to ensure that the nation’s largest lenders can seamlessly draw on its Discount Window Facility (DWF) during temporary liquidity shortages.
While the mandate focuses on systemically vital institutions, smaller banks will also be strongly encouraged to adopt identical operational protocols.

The DWF acts as a short-term credit backstop designed to protect financial stability when commercial cash squeezes occur, functioning alongside rather than replacing individual bank liquidity management.

To implement the mandate, the BSP has proposed a three-month transition window from the circular’s effective date, giving major lenders a strict timeline to set up and maintain active DWF credit lines.
Institutions that currently hold or have pending applications for DWF lines will fall under the new regulatory framework immediately upon implementation.
As part of the proposed overhaul, the central bank is removing several administrative hurdles that previously slowed down credit approvals and line renewals.

Under the revised guidelines, local financial institutions will primarily need to satisfy a simplified standard requiring no outstanding default under existing DWF agreements to keep their credit facilities active.

To prevent delays during sudden market stress, the BSP is pushing lenders to establish a proactive collateral framework. Rather than waiting for liquidity constraints to materialize, banks are being urged to preposition credit instruments with the central bank for pre-verification, ensuring rapid drawdown capabilities when emergency funding is needed.

The BSP is also set to ease strict oversight mechanisms on select transactions, notably those tied to real estate property, in an effort to streamline overall facility access and reduce friction in emergency lending channels.

articles.title: DTI: Philippine exports to beat targets as electronics, services demand rallies
articles.summary: The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) expects export growth to beat moderate forecasts this year as overseas demand for Philippine products keeps climbing. Citing the latest trade figures,…

blocks.text: The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) expects export growth to beat moderate forecasts this year as overseas demand for Philippine products keeps climbing.

Citing the latest trade figures, DTI-Export Marketing Bureau (EMB) Director Bianca Sykimte said the agency is optimistic that total exports will outperform the lower targets set by the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC).
“We are cautiously optimistic that we'll surpass that forecast,” Sykimte told reporters last week.
Last month, the DBCC projected a three percent increase in merchandise exports and four percent growth in service exports for the year.
The Department of Budget and Management (DBM), which chairs the DBCC, noted that international trade will likely stay moderate due to an expected global slowdown.
The DBM attributed the cooling market to normalizing inventory cycles and potential supply chain snarls driven by geopolitical tensions.
“We're still doing the numbers, but we're optimistic that we're going to grow,” Sykimte said.

Preliminary data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) showed that goods exports jumped nearly 13 percent to $54.92 billion from January to July from $48.67 billion in the same period last year.
Electronics remained the country’s primary export driver, bringing in $30.92 billion, or over 63 percent of the total.
Meanwhile, first-quarter service exports grew four percent year-on-year, rising to $12.79 billion from $12.26 billion.
To build on this momentum, Sykimte said the DTI is urging local exporters to capitalize on existing free trade agreements (FTAs) and preferential trading deals.
She specifically cited the United Kingdom's Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS), which local businesses have yet to fully leverage.
According to UK trade adviser Ellie Parker, roughly £92 million (around ₱7.7 billion) in eligible exports failed to take advantage of the DCTS’s lower tariff rates.

To boost participation, Sykimte said Manila is partnering with London to market the program, focusing heavily on sectors with the lowest utilization rates. The DCTS slashes tariffs, removes trade conditions, and streamlines rules for developing nations.
However, the Philippines will eventually transition out of the program if it maintains its upper-middle-income status for three consecutive years.
Sykimte hinted that the government may pursue a bilateral FTA with the UK after aging out of the scheme, ensuring local goods continue to enjoy preferential tariffs.
“Market diversification has always been a strategy for us, so we’re doing our best to promote all these FTAs,” she said.

articles.title: DigiPlus partnership, LaVie upgrades drive IEC’s Philippine gaming expansion
articles.summary: Hong Kong-listed International Entertainment Corp. (IEC) is banking on the expansion of LaVie Resort & Casino Manila and its entry into online gaming with DigiPlus Interactive Corp. to drive growth…

blocks.text: Hong Kong-listed International Entertainment Corp. (IEC) is banking on the expansion of LaVie Resort & Casino Manila and its entry into online gaming with DigiPlus Interactive Corp. to drive growth in the Philippines despite expectations of softer near-term momentum in the local gaming sector.

In an Aug. 28 statement, IEC said it remains optimistic about the long-term prospects of the Philippine gaming and tourism sectors, citing the country’s strategic position in Southeast Asia, supportive government policies and rising status as a travel destination.
The company, however, said short-term momentum in the Philippine gaming sector may soften amid geopolitical tensions and muted consumer spending.

IEC’s indirect wholly owned subsidiary New Coast Leisure Inc. (NCLI) signed a cooperation agreement on June 9 with Total Gamezone Xtreme Inc. (TGXI), a wholly owned subsidiary of DigiPlus, for LaVie’s online gaming operations.

Under the agreement, the companies will collaborate on the integration, aggregation, provision, technical support and operation of approved online games and related gaming content through or in connection with LaVie’s online gaming platform and operations, subject to regulatory approvals.
IEC said participation in online gaming is expected to broaden its revenue base, improve operational scalability and create new growth drivers.

The agreement would allow IEC to leverage TGXI’s existing online gaming infrastructure as it expands LaVie into digital gaming. The cooperation is non-exclusive and remains subject to Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (Pagcor) approval and other applicable regulatory requirements.

IEC has also expanded LaVie’s land-based gaming operations, completing renovation works on the casino’s ground floor in January. The additional gaming space allowed the property to accommodate more gaming tables and slot machines.
In May, IEC entered into another construction contract worth about HK$72.17 million for improvements to the hotel following the first two phases of construction works initiated last year.
The company said the latest renovations are intended to modernize outdated amenities and improve the hotel’s facilities, with the upgrades expected to support future casino and hotel revenue.

DigiPlus, meanwhile, fully paid its HK$1.6-billion, or about ₱12-billion, subscription to IEC convertible notes in June after settling the second HK$800-million tranche. The first HK$800-million tranche was completed in March.
The five-year convertible notes carry an annual interest rate of three percent. Upon full conversion, DigiPlus would hold a 53.89-percent majority stake in IEC.

DigiPlus has yet to convert the notes into equity, with the investment positioning the company to eventually take control of IEC and add a physical casino and hotel operation to its predominantly digital gaming business.
“Looking ahead, the group is strategically positioned to capture the next phase of growth in the Philippine gaming and tourism sectors,” IEC said.
IEC’s expansion comes as its gaming business recorded strong growth in its latest fiscal year (FY).

Gaming revenue surged 60.7 percent to HK$819.4 million during the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, driven by its land-based casino operations and provision of a gaming platform to other authorized gaming operators.
Overall revenue increased by 50.6 percent to HK$852.5 million, while gross profit jumped 66.4 percent to HK$454.6 million.
The company’s gross profit margin widened by five percentage points (ppts) to 53.3 percent from 48.3 percent a year ago.
Hotel operations, however, generated lower revenue of HK$33.1 million from HK$56.2 million a year ago due to the temporary closure of some rooms for renovation.
IEC reported a loss attributable to owners of HK$486.4 million, wider than the HK$282.1-million loss a year ago due partly to a non-cash loss from changes in the fair value of convertible notes.
Excluding the non-cash fair-value loss, IEC said its attributable loss narrowed by about 78.2 percent from a year ago.

articles.title: Philippine peso Asia’s worst-performing currency—Japanese bank
articles.summary: The Philippine peso sank to a record low against the US dollar, making it Asia’s worst-performing currency over the past week as soaring energy import costs and widening trade deficit offset recent…

blocks.text: The Philippine peso sank to a record low against the US dollar, making it Asia’s worst-performing currency over the past week as soaring energy import costs and widening trade deficit offset recent central bank rate hikes.
In an Aug. 28 commentary, Japanese lender MUFG Bank Ltd. noted that the peso’s underperformance stems from persistent pressure on the nation’s external account.
The local currency closed at ₱62.265 per dollar on Friday, Aug. 28, sinking past its previous historic low of ₱61.888 set just a day earlier.

Data from the Bankers Association of the Philippines showed the peso opened at ₱62.05 before hitting an intraday low of ₱62.27, driven by a surge in safe-haven demand amid rising geopolitical tensions.

The peso lost one percent for the week, extending a broader slide. According to MUFG, the currency is down 1.6 percent since the start of August, 1.4 percent for the current quarter, and 5.8 percent year-to-date—continuing a multi-year slump from 2024 and 2025.
The Thai baht also dropped 0.8 percent during the week. “Both currencies remained vulnerable to concerns over external balances, softer growth momentum and sensitivity to energy prices,” MUFG stated.
In contrast, the South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar gained 1.1 percent and 0.8 percent, respectively, against the greenback.

“Both currencies were supported by continued enthusiasm around the AI and semiconductor cycle, which boosted sentiment towards North Asian technology exporters and helped attract equity inflows,” MUFG added.
The Malaysian ringgit and Indian rupee also edged higher, backed by relatively stable domestic economic conditions.

To counter mounting pressures, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) raised its benchmark policy rate by 25 basis points to five percent, marking its third consecutive hike aimed at reining in sticky inflation.

Headline inflation slowed to a three-month low of 6.2 percent in July from 6.4 percent in June, down from its peak of 7.2 percent in April. Core inflation—which excludes volatile food and energy items—eased to 4.2 percent from 4.4 percent.
Despite the tighter policy stance, the peso’s decline accelerated after government data showed July imports jumped 59.7 percent, blowing out the trade deficit to roughly $6 billion, MUFG noted.

These widening imbalances and elevated commodity prices are expected to keep monetary authorities cautious. “Persistent inflation, a widening external deficit and peso weakness leave the BSP open to further tightening, albeit at a slower pace,” the bank said.
MUFG added that upcoming implementation of record-high wage adjustments presents additional upside risks to inflation, keeping the door open for another 25-basis-point hike.

Looking ahead, MUFG forecasts the peso to recover to ₱61.75 per dollar this quarter, strengthen to ₱61.5 in the fourth quarter, reach ₱61 by the first quarter of 2027, and move into the mid-₱60 range by the second quarter of 2027.

articles.title: Gov’t eyes higher biodiesel blend in 2027 as coconut oil prices ease
articles.summary: The government is expected to increase the country’s biodiesel blend next year once prices of coco methyl ester (CME) stabilize at a level that would not further burden motorists, according to the…

blocks.text: The government is expected to increase the country’s biodiesel blend next year once prices of coco methyl ester (CME) stabilize at a level that would not further burden motorists, according to the Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA).

PCA Administrator and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Dexter Buted said the Department of Agriculture (DA)-attached agency has recommended increasing the biodiesel mandate from three percent to five percent, or B3 to B5, to the Department of Energy (DOE).
The DOE oversees adjustments in the biodiesel blend based on the recommendation of the interagency National Biofuels Board (NBB), which it chairs.
“We’re pushing the DOE and also the government, but it will depend on the price of the CME,” Buted said in an interview last week.
CME biodiesel is currently averaging around ₱135 per liter, while diesel prices are fetching ₱77 to ₱97.50 per liter, based on the latest DOE monitoring in Metro Manila.
Buted said higher CME prices are the main reason why the government has not yet raised the biodiesel blend despite strong industry demand.
The DA recently endorsed a policy resolution calling for an immediate transition to B5, which seeks to gradually reduce fuel costs and generate greater value for the coconut sector.
CME is seeing higher prices amid growing demand for coconut oil in the global market as countries look to secure alternative sources amid the ongoing energy crisis.
Coconut oil is the main feedstock of CME, which is the raw material used to produce biodiesel.
There is some optimism that coconut oil prices are now trending downward, having fallen in June to below $2,000 per metric ton (MT) for the first time in 16 months.
The latest World Bank data showed that the average price of coconut oil in the global market was $1,924 per MT in July, down by nearly three percent from $1,979 per MT in June.
“If the price declines, I guess there will be no reason why the government should not impose the five percent of the biodiesel,” said Buted.
Buted said PCA expects prices of CME biodiesel to stabilize by next year, although he said he cannot yet project whether this would happen in the early or latter part of the year.
To prepare for the eventual increase in the biodiesel blend, PCA is actively promoting programs to strengthen the productivity of the coconut sector.
Citing industry estimates, Buted said local production right now is enough to support a potential increase in the blend to up to seven percent, or B7.
He said the country’s coconut output this year is on track to grow by five percent from last year’s total production of 14.51 million MT.
If this is realized, coconut production would exceed 15 million MT for the first time in 13 years.

articles.title: World Bank: Philippines ‘policy-rich but implementation-poor’ on disaster-risk planning
articles.summary: The Philippines has built one of the most formally developed systems for integrating disaster and climate risks into land-use planning among developing countries, but weak enforcement, uneven local…

blocks.text: The Philippines has built one of the most formally developed systems for integrating disaster and climate risks into land-use planning among developing countries, but weak enforcement, uneven local government capacity, as well as political interference continue to undermine its implementation, according to the World Bank.

In two reports dated May 26 and published last Friday, Aug. 28, the Washington-based multilateral lender described the country’s approach as “policy-rich but implementation-poor,” reflecting the persistent gap between its extensive planning framework and implementation on the ground.

The World Bank said smaller municipalities—which often face greater exposure to natural hazards but have fewer resources—struggle to meet even the basic requirements of a compliant climate and disaster risk assessment (CDRA), while highly urbanized as well as better-resourced local government units (LGUs) benefit more from the system’s strengths.

The findings were contained in “Building Resilience into the Blueprint: What Works, What Doesn’t, and Why? Insights from Asia-Pacific Countries on Risk-Informed Spatial Planning” and its accompanying country case studies, which examined the Philippines alongside Australia, China, as well as South Korea.

According to the World Bank, the Philippines has established one of the most legally comprehensive risk-informed spatial planning frameworks in Asia-Pacific. Its system requires disaster and climate risks to be incorporated into comprehensive land use plans (CLUPs), which serve as LGUs’ primary instruments for regulating land use.

CDRA, meanwhile, incorporates hazard, exposure, and vulnerability indicators to produce risk maps that are fed into CLUPs and zoning ordinances, as well as comprehensive development plans (CDPs), local disaster risk reduction and management plans (LDRRMPs), as well as local climate change action plans (LCCAPs).

Despite this framework, the World Bank identified enforcement as the system’s “most critical weakness,” citing that zoning ordinances and risk-informed plans are applied inconsistently, particularly in resource-constrained LGUs that lack technical personnel, financing, or political will to enforce controls against powerful development interests.

The report also warned that political pressures and institutional inertia continue to allow development in high-risk areas, while informal settlements in hazard-prone locations largely bypass the formal permitting system, leaving many vulnerable communities outside the protection intended by land-use regulations.

Another structural problem is the proliferation of planning requirements. The World Bank cited that LGUs are required to produce more than 30 mandated sectoral plans with different formats, schedules, and institutional owners, contributing to “planning fatigue” that can weaken the quality of individual plans.

It added that the absence of a National Land Use Act (NaLUA), which the report noted has stalled in Congress for more than three decades, continues to deprive the Philippines of a unified legislative foundation for spatial planning.

Without a NaLUA, the integration of disaster risk into spatial planning remains dependent in part on agency guidelines and executive issuances that are “inherently more fragile than law,” the World Bank said.

The report also raised concern over what it called a growing “science-policy time lag,” noting that many existing CLUPs as well as CDRA guidelines remain based on the United Nations’ (UN) Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) fourth assessment report (AR4) climate scenarios, even as newer AR5 and AR6 projections have become available.

The newer projections, including more granular regional data as well as updated estimates for extreme events, have yet to be systematically integrated into standard planning guidance and training, raising the risk that existing plans could underestimate future exposure to sea-level rise, heavier rainfall, and stronger storm surges.

Many LGUs also lack tenured geographic information system (GIS) specialists, risk assessment analysts, as well as qualified urban planners, making them dependent on private consultants and limiting their ability to build permanent in-house expertise, the report said.

High personnel turnover following local elections also regularly erodes institutional memory and disrupts continuity between planning cycles, while efforts to professionalize local planning through licensure, civil service reforms, as well as protected technical positions have progressed slowly.

The World Bank likewise flagged the discretionary authority of local zoning boards to grant exceptions and variances from risk-based zoning rules, saying that this creates a pathway for scientific risk assessments to be overridden by political or economic pressure.

The problem is particularly pronounced in rapidly developing peri-urban areas, or those in the outskirts of cities, where rising land values can put landowner and developer interests in conflict with restrictions intended to limit construction in high-risk locations.

The World Bank said legally enforceable risk controls are essential because hazard information treated merely as advisory can be disregarded amid pressure to allow development. It recommended stronger national legislation, formal coordination between disaster-risk and planning agencies, improved local technical capacity, as well as mechanisms to insulate technical land-use decisions from short-term political pressure.

For highly decentralized systems like the Philippines, the report said sustained technical assistance (TA), standardized tools, as well as meaningful national oversight are particularly important to prevent wide variations in plan quality and merely superficial compliance with national requirements.

The World Bank credited the Philippines with having one of the most formally developed disaster- and climate-risk planning systems in the developing world, supported by CDRA and digital platforms such as PlanSmart for sustainable human settlements, geospatial information management and analysis project for hazards and risk assessment in the Philippines (GeoRiskPH), University of the Philippines nationwide operational assessment of hazards (UP-NOAH), and rapid earthquake damage assessment system (REDAS).

It cited the cities of Davao, Iloilo, and Tagbilaran as examples where local political commitment and technical capacity have translated risk-informed planning into flood-protection infrastructure, publicly accessible hazard-overlay zoning maps, as well as building permit systems that provide site-specific risk guidance.

The report also noted that the mandatory five-percent local disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) budget allocation, which, when linked to an approved LDRRMP, provides a structural fiscal commitment for risk-reduction measures.

articles.title: Marcos admin’s gross borrowings breach ₱2.1 trillion mark at end-July
articles.summary: The Marcos administration accelerated its fundraising drive in July, pushing total gross borrowings past the ₱2 trillion mark for the first seven months of the year. According to the Bureau of the…

blocks.text: The Marcos administration accelerated its fundraising drive in July, pushing total gross borrowings past the ₱2 trillion mark for the first seven months of the year.
According to the Bureau of the Treasury, gross financing reached ₱2.11 trillion in January to July, a 20 percent expansion compared with the ₱1.76 trillion recorded in the same period in 2025.

The July accumulation alone added ₱291.4 billion to government liabilities. With five months remaining in the fiscal year, President Marcos has already executed more than 77 percent of the government’s full-year borrowing plan of ₱2.73 trillion.
The steady accumulation was also a reversal from earlier in the second quarter when fiscal authorities temporarily dialed back market issuances in April and May.
The momentum rebuilt rapidly heading into midyear, anchored by a record-setting ₱579.6 billion issuance in June that drew heavily from both onshore and offshore investors.

Local capital markets provided the bulk of the financing, with domestic lenders supplying ₱1.55 trillion—or 73.3 percent—of total gross borrowings through July. That reflects a 15.4 percent increase from the ₱1.34 trillion raised locally during the comparative period last year.
Domestic activity gained noticeable speed in July alone, with the Treasury securing ₱271.3 billion, nearly double the ₱152.5 billion raised in July 2025.

To absorb investor demand across the yield curve, the Treasury leaned heavily on long-term paper while expanding short-term issues. Fixed-rate Treasury bonds accounted for ₱1.16 trillion of the seven-month domestic total, up almost one-third from ₱881.8 billion a year earlier. Simultaneously, net issuance of short-dated Treasury bills soared to ₱390.9 billion, more than doubling the ₱159.9 billion recorded in the first seven months of 2025.

Although the domestic share of total borrowing rebounded from 70.1 percent at end-June to 73.3 percent by late July, it remains below the national government’s target mix of 77 percent onshore financing.

On the external front, gross foreign liabilities expanded by more than a third to ₱564.9 billion. Offshore fundraising was heavily front-loaded into two major transactions: a ₱161.3 billion multi-tranche global bond deal in January and a ₱153.1 billion triple-tranche offshore offering in June. Having concluded its offshore bond program midyear, the Marcos administration relies on project loans from foreign institutions to complete its external mandate.
Official development assistance and project financing reached ₱92.9 billion by late July, a 78.8 percent increase from ₱51.9 billion a year ago.
With the foreign bond pipeline tapped out for the remainder of the year to support the ₱6.793 trillion national budget, fiscal managers are shifting full focus to domestic creditors.

The Treasury plans to auction ₱1.12 trillion in local debt instruments during the third quarter, a 40 percent jump from the prior quarter, as it navigates volatile global interest rate conditions by anchoring its strategy to shorter-dated paper.

articles.title: IFC approves $170-million investment in YCO Cloud’s Philippine data center expansion
articles.summary: International Finance Corp. (IFC), the World Bank Group’s (WBG) private-sector lending arm, has approved up to $170 million in financing for YCO Global Cloud Centers Holdings Inc. (YCO Cloud),…

blocks.text: International Finance Corp. (IFC), the World Bank Group’s (WBG) private-sector lending arm, has approved up to $170 million in financing for YCO Global Cloud Centers Holdings Inc. (YCO Cloud), confirming a major investment in the Philippine data center developer first reported by Manila Bulletin in May.
World Bank board minutes disclosed last Friday, Aug. 28, showed that the board of directors approved the financing for the YCO Catalyst Project on July 28 on an absence-of-objection basis.

The approved package consists of a mezzanine loan investment of up to $20 million in YCO Cloud and senior A loans totaling as much as $150 million, or its Philippine peso equivalent, to special purpose project companies owned by the platform.
The minutes also showed that WBG executive director Robert Bruce Nicholl and alternate executive director Sandro Maluck abstained from the decision.

The approval confirms Manila Bulletin’s report last May that IFC was preparing an investment package of up to $170 million to support YCO Cloud’s expansion amid growing demand for data center capacity in the Philippines.
The YCO Catalyst Project has an estimated total cost of $1.054 billion, with the IFC financing intended to support the development of the company’s data center platform in the country.
YCO Cloud plans to develop two data centers in Malvar town, Batangas province, with a combined capacity of 50 megawatts (MW), alongside another facility in Bataan province.

The Malvar 1 and 2 data centers, both located within an industrial park in Batangas, have already been constructed, while the Bataan facility was still in the planning stage when IFC disclosed the proposed investment in May.

Supporting infrastructure for the planned Bataan facility, including a transmission line, water supply plant, as well as wastewater treatment facility, is expected to be built by the industrial park and the government for the site’s exclusive use.

IFC earlier said the investment is expected to expand businesses’ access to data hosting services, support the growth of digital services, and improve productivity. It could also strengthen competition in the Philippine data-hosting market and help narrow supply gaps.
IFC also intends to help ensure that YCO Cloud’s facilities meet international standards for energy efficiency and environmental sustainability.
YCO Cloud is majority owned by the Ynchausti family, which holds an 82-percent stake in the company, while Sy-led conglomerate SM Investments Corp. (SMIC) is a minority shareholder.

YCO Cloud is led by president and co-founder Nik de Ynchausti. Its leadership team also includes former presidential deputy spokesperson Abigail Valte as chief legal officer, while former Senate president Franklin Drilon serves as senior advisor, according to the company’s website.

De Ynchausti earlier said the company’s “mission-critical infrastructure is designed to position the Philippines to be Southeast Asia’s digital hub within the next two decades, re-establishing it as the region’s gateway to the West” through “sustainable, greenfield, carrier-neutral, and flexible data center facilities.”

articles.title: Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right
articles.summary: The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has embarked on a confrontational course toward the churches. Representatives of the Catholic and Protestant churches are responding with a mix of anxiety and resolve.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt's churches have been reminding voters of their Christian values ahead of the state election on September 6Image: Christoph Strack/DW

blocks.text: Flags flutter in the wind outside Magdeburg's Catholic cathedral. "Love thy neighbor, dialogue, human dignity, solidarity. VOTE CONSCIOUSLY!", they proclaim. Just a few minutes' walk away, a sign on the building of the Protestant Cathedral Congregation reads: "DIVERSITY IS DIVINE." Other Protestant churches across the region display banners reading "Heart Instead of Hate."

For many months now, warnings about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is particularly strong in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, have been part of everyday church life. During a sermon at a pilgrimage event in September 2025, Magdeburg Bishop Gerhard Feige remarked almost in passing that pilgrims of hope do not cast their votes on a whim, "into the blue." He was interrupted by prolonged applause — blue is the AfD's party color.

The AfD holds a commanding lead in the polls ahead of the state election on September 6. The prospect of a government led by the party alone appears increasingly plausible. At the same time, Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Churches speak out against AfD
In Saxony-Anhalt, 10% of the population is Protestant and 3% is Catholic; only a few thousand people belong to the Muslim or Jewish faiths.

More than 85% of the state's 2.1 million residents have no religious affiliation, compared with a national average of 47%. Nevertheless, the churches play an important role as defenders of democracy — and that, apparently, is precisely what troubles the AfD.

With its so-called government program, adopted at a state party conference in April, the party launched a broadside against both the Protestant and Catholic churches. The program calls for an end to all state payments to the two churches and for the abolition of church tax collection by public authorities, a service for which the churches themselves pay.

blocks.caption: Bishop Gerhard Feige has said he could never have imagined that so many people could once again be so easily led astray by the far rightImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In cases of so-called church asylum, where refugees seek shelter on church premises for fear of renewed persecution in their countries of origin, the AfD is calling for churches to be held financially accountable on a "permanent" basis.

The Protestant Academy of Saxony-Anhalt should also no longer receive any state funding whatsoever. The reason, according to the AfD, is its "political agitation in line with the established parties: climate dogma, gender ideology, and the rainbow cult." The academy is said to advocate "unchecked mass immigration." Yet in scarcely any German federal state is the proportion of foreign nationals as low as it is in Saxony-Anhalt.
From estrangement to open confrontation

The sharpness of the criticism goes far beyond anything typically heard from other regional branches of the Alternative for Germany or from the party's national leadership. Long gone are the days when representatives of the then-emerging party complained about not being invited to church congresses or Catholic conventions.

In February 2024, the plenary assembly of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference unanimously adopted a declaration entitled "Ethnic Nationalism and Christianity are Incompatible." In it, the bishops identified an ethnonationalist mindset within the AfD and spoke of a "genuine right-wing extremism." The document was prompted by the state elections scheduled to take place later that year in the eastern German states of Thuringia, Saxony, and Brandenburg. Now, in September 2026, elections are due to follow in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
At present, the confrontation between the AfD and the churches is nowhere more intense than in Saxony-Anhalt.
Germany's churches get creative about new ways to worship

For Bishop Feige, the AfD's current direction is "without question" an expression of ethnonationalism. "Until now, Saxony-Anhalt's motto has been 'Thinking Modern'. The AfD wants to replace it with 'Thinking German'," he told DW. "The AfD's election posters speak a very clear language: 'Save your country', 'Take your country back', 'Deport from day one!' What else could that be but ethnonationalism?"

The 74-year-old said he "could never have imagined that so many people today could once again be so easily led astray, or that arsonists, pied pipers and respectable-looking agitators could emerge, and that so many would fall for them."

As an example, Feige cited the so-called flag assembly that the AfD wants to reintroduce in the state's schools: the raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem. "This existed during the Nazi era and was later adopted by the GDR," he said, referring to the former East Germany. "And now it is supposed to return? I find that inconceivable."

blocks.caption: Bishop Friedrich Kramer said Christian messages should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political partyImage: Martin Schutt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both major Christian churches emphasize they are speaking out not against a particular party, but in defense of a Christian view of humanity. Whether the issue is climate protection and the safeguarding of creation or the treatment of strangers, the churches' interventions are "primarily not political messages, but Christian ones, and should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party," Friedrich Kramer, bishop of the Protestant Church in central Germany, recently told the online magazine Die Eule.
Religious freedom, according to the AfD

Jews and Jewish life, incidentally, are never mentioned in the government program. By contrast, Islam appears repeatedly. According to the AfD, it will "restore religious freedom to appropriate limits." Islam is described as a "religion alien to our culture." Freedom of religion, the party argues, does not oblige Germans to "fulfill every demand of the Islamic lobby."

Representatives of the state's Jewish association, which includes the synagogue of the Jewish community of Halle targeted in a 2019 right-wing extremist attack, as well as representatives of the largest mosque congregation in the state, declined to comment when asked.

Notably, the AfD's platform speaks of a "Christian mission" that, in its view, the churches supported by church tax, which it labels the "church-tax churches," no longer fulfill. This evokes the support that US President Donald Trump receives from influential evangelical and conservative Christian groups in the United States. In Saxony-Anhalt, however, there is only a limited presence of comparable religious milieus.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?
Why bishops are sounding the alarm

"A government involving the AfD would have devastating consequences," Kramer said. That is why, he added, cultural institutions and civil society organizations are joining forces to warn against the AfD.

His Catholic counterpart, Feige, likewise cautioned against "downplaying" the prospect of an AfD-led government. During the election campaign, he said, the party is presenting itself "with messianic ideas" and promoting slogans such as "Everything will be fine" or "Anything is possible."

Because the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, "comes across as highly polished and enthusiastic," some people ask what could possibly be "right-wing extremist or dangerous" about him. "But behind him stand forces that give cause for concern," said Feige. "If an AfD single-party government comes to power here, it will be a pilot project. Then Saxony-Anhalt will become a gateway to national politics."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Cone savors 'sweet' Gilas win over Iran, home sweep
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines–Coach Tim Cone considers himself the “happiest guy in the world” after Gilas Pilipinas completed a fourth window sweep of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers with Sunday’s 68-56…

blocks.text: Gilas Pilipinas coach Tim Cone during a game against Iran in the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers at Mall of Asia Arena.–MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net

MANILA, Philippines–Coach Tim Cone considers himself the “happiest guy in the world” after Gilas Pilipinas completed a fourth window sweep of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers with Sunday’s 68-56 win over Iran.
Gilas improved to an even 4-4 win-loss slate before a home crowd at Mall of Asia Arena, trimming the gap with Iran, and also Jordan after the two teams fell to 5-3 to close out the window winless.
The Philippines defeated Jordan, 82-81, in overtime last Friday.

Cone also took notice of the circumstances behind Gilas’ win, as it beat Iran for the first time in a Fiba competition since the 2015 Asian Championship in Changsha, China, while also playing with an all-Filipino lineup following the absence of naturalized player Justin Brownlee.
“It makes it really sweet to come out and win this game,” said Cone.
But Gilas had to go the wringer for the second straight game after missing 11 of 13 shots in the first quarter to trail 18-7.
Big contributions from Kai Sotto, Juan Gomez de Liano, plus a morale-boosting appearance from the retiring June Mar Fajardo enabled Gilas to fight back and turn the contest into a seesaw affair.
It wasn’t until the fourth quarter that Ramos made crucial shots, even as the rest of Gilas was able to tighten things up to see off the Iranian side.

“It was one of those slow starts that we have, but the guys kept fighting and fighting and getting back into the game,” Cone said. “At halftime, we felt good about ourselves, and we felt we could pull this one out.
“But it’s just a great character performance by these guys, in both games,” he added.

articles.title: Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research
articles.summary:
Nathan Cofnas allowed to resume Ghent University work, as US ambassador claims credit for lifting of suspension

Prof Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on…

blocks.text: Prof Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.
Earlier this month Cofnas, an American academic, was suspended from his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.

Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.
In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.

The US ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.

In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.

Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been mired in controversy. In May, Ghent’s philosophy department alleged to university leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise” for his role researching “the future of liberalism”, alleging he had a “far-right agenda”.

In July Cofnas accused Arday, a Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August. His family paid tribute to him as an “amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.

blocks.caption: Jason Arday was found dead on 14 August. He was accused of plagiarism by Cofnas.  Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: White, a Donald Trump supporter, donor and fundraiser, had called Cofnas’s suspension “truly unacceptable”, calling for De Sutter to immediately rescind it earlier this month.

On Friday, White wrote on his personal X account: “I just saved Belgium from a complete global media meltdown and well deserved spanking by @elonmusk and everyone by resolving the UGHENT Cofnas matter – quite quickly.”

The night before, Cofnas thanked White and the US state department for “defending American values” on X, adding: “It was beyond my imagination that such a person would take an interest in the fate of a postdoc. The Ambassador responded with great support which helped to bring about a just outcome.”

“Anti-woke” Cofnas has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, and was reportedly among bloggers recommended to the Palantir founder, Peter Thiel, by a “race science” researcher.
Cofnas has also hit out at Trump and Maga in his writing, while claiming the US president’s executive orders against diversity, equity and inclusion in the US were a “cause for celebration”.
In a piece in April last year he said the Republican party had “degenerated into a low-IQ cult of personality”.

Hitting out at Trump’s tariffs, he said the effect “will be to halt the American economic juggernaut, discredit the anti-woke movement, pave the way for a leftwing populist … (and) stop the right’s momentum in other countries”.

In October, he wrote: “The right simply does not have the human capital to retake the institutions and run them effectively. The vast majority of intelligent, psychologically stable, and public-spirited Americans remain left and woke. The Trump administration’s war on universities, science, and data has only reinforced smart people’s identity as leftists.”

Asked by the Guardian if he stood by previous criticisms of Trump and Maga, Cofnas said: “I voted for Trump three times and I am still a registered Republican. I strongly criticised some Maga policies, particularly tariffs. There are other Maga policies that I support, such as interventions on behalf of free speech.”

Ghent University said it did “not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding this matter … ongoing preliminary disciplinary inquiries must be allowed to proceed calmly, independently and with full respect for the rights of all those involved”.

articles.title: June Mar Fajardo sparks Gilas Pilipinas win in his 'last game'
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines–June Mar Fajardo officially confirmed his retirement from Gilas Pilipinas duties following Sunday’s 68-56 win over Iran in the fourth window of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers…

blocks.text: June Mar Fajardo holds up the game ball as he says goodbye to the crowd after playing his final game for Gilas Pilipinas–a 68-56 win over Iran in the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers–on Sunday at Mall of Asia Arena.–MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net

MANILA, Philippines–June Mar Fajardo officially confirmed his retirement from Gilas Pilipinas duties following Sunday’s 68-56 win over Iran in the fourth window of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers at Mall of Asia Arena.
And Fajardo made sure that he won’t go off into the sunset without having a hand in the victory that enabled Gilas to close in on the race for spots in next year’s World Cup in Doha, Qatar.
Fajardo had six points and two rebounds in seven minutes, but it was during the second quarter when he helped spark Gilas’ fightback from a lethargic first quarter.

THANK YOU, JMF 🥹 June Mar Fajardo receives “MVP” chants in what might be his last game for Gilas Pilipinas. @inquirersports pic.twitter.com/i3vouiDwFX — Rommel Fuertes Jr. (@MeloFuertesINQ) August 30, 2026

“Siyempre kung ano yung pwede kung maitulong, ibibigay ko kasi gusto ko i-cherish yung last game ko (Of course, I wanted to give whatever I can to help because I want to cherish my last game),” Fajardo said.
A jump hook over Arman Zangeneh with 2:39 left that cut the deficit to 29-25 brought big cheers from the crowd, and the basket seemed to have galvanized Gilas.
Coach Tim Cone later said that the play was a morale-booster for the home side, which would go into the half up 36-34 after trailing 18-5 in the opening period.

Gilas would eventually get the job done behind Kai Sotto, Juan Gomez de Liano, Dwight Ramos and AJ Edu, allowing Fajardo to get a fitting curtain call with chants of “MVP” and receive the game ball from his teammates.

‘LAST GAME NA. LAST GAME NA TALAGA’ 👏 After 13 years of representing the Philippines with Gilas, June Mar Fajardo officially calls it a career. @inquirersports pic.twitter.com/tCPss9VjKy — Rommel Fuertes Jr. (@MeloFuertesINQ) August 30, 2026
The swan song was actually his 70th game in all Fiba competitions across 13 years that started at the same venue in the 2013 Fiba Asia Championship.
And with that, Fajardo’s national team career has come full circle.
“Last game, last game na talaga (it’s really my last game),” said the 36-year-old Fajardo.
