His wife, Manjula Atmakur, who arrived in Kathmandu to search for him on Friday, told the newspaper she was disappointed by the British government’s response to the disaster.
Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers in its group who were unaccounted for.

blocks.caption: Family members of missing flood victims look at the list of missing people at the emergency ward of the Maharajgunj medical campus in Kathmandu. Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty

blocks.text: Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list. “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there,” he said. “She must be in trauma.”

Also missing are an A-level student from Surrey, Spandan Sahu, 18, and his father, Santosh Sahu, 46, the chief executive of the UK pharmaceutical technology company Charac; Spandan’s mother, Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44; and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.
Mahadev Semwal, a friend of Sahu’s for about 15 years, said: “I had WhatsApp communication with him on Monday: they were going to Nepal then Manasarovar in Tibet.
“When I heard on Wednesday about the flooding, I lost contact with him – when I am trying to message him it is getting delivered but not read.
“Our heart says they are safe somewhere. It’s possible because the communication is jammed.
“But when you see the videos, it is unbelievable. It feels so bad.”
Also confirmed missing was Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse from Dartford, Kent, who left for Nepal last Saturday on a religious journey.

Deepesh Patel told the Press Association that his parents, Bipin Patel, 66, and Mala Patel, 60, from Coventry, were missing after flying to Nepal on 22 August for a pilgrimage. His brother Anant Patel told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information on their whereabouts.
Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he had not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.
“We’re not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week,” Kolagatla added.

Tatjana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she had not been able to contact her sister, Julija Jakovicka, who was attending a yoga and meditation retreat near the Nepal-Tibet border when flash flooding hit.
Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he had not heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, or sister-in-law, Ankita Chandra, 35, who had gone on a pilgrimage.
Ranjan added: “We don’t know if they crossed the border … We don’t have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated.”

The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said it had been unable to make contact with a party of 12 Britons aged 13 to 65 who had booked a tour to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and were in the vicinity when the flash floods hit.

blocks.caption: Firefighters conduct search and rescue operations at a damaged area in Gyirong county, Tibet. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: Sunil Amin, from Croydon in south London, shared with the Daily Mail the “horrible, horrible feeling” of repeatedly trying to phone his wife, Hema Amin, 63, who was on a pilgrimage with Alpine Eco Trek from Nepal to Tibet with her sister. “I’m devastated,” he said.

The Trekkers’ Society, which organises tours across Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage had gone missing. The organisation confirmed that four men and boys aged between 14 and 50 and five women aged 40 to 53 were unaccounted for.

Himalayan Glacier US said it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff, including two Britons, who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, regarded as the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.
The tour operator Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – who were travelling with it.

Leaf Holidays, which runs Himalayan treks and expeditions from Kathmandu, wrote in a Facebook post that its group of 55 travellers remained missing, including four British citizens, Tara and Babar Gurung and Thaneswar and Tejkumari Gurung, who have not been heard from since Tuesday.

Twelve of the missing British citizens were on a tour to Mount Kailash led by Nabhi Nandan Das, a 64-year-old Hindu priest who works at the Sanatan Mandir and community centre in Surrey, the Telegraph reported. He is understood to have been leading 11 Britons on a tour that was due to visit Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, two Hindu holy sites in Tibet.

blocks.caption: People wait for information about their missing relatives outside a military camp in the Trishuli area of Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Pramod Poudel, who runs a Nepalese street food company in Sussex, told the Daily Mail his wife, Sumitra, mother, Tulisa, brother Pradip and uncle Madav were all missing. His father, Purusottam, has been found alive.
The Non-Resident Nepali Association in the UK launched an emergency fundraising appeal on Thursday and more than £12,000 has been raised.
Rajendra Pudasaini, a nurse in Essex who is president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss” and Nepal was “paying the price for global warming”.

Pudasaini told BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme that many of his family members were missing. “My godson, we found the body yesterday morning, you know, he (was) just buried under the mud at his house, and yes, lots of other dead bodies being found.”
He added: “It’s a very difficult situation to describe, actually.”

articles.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
articles.summary:
Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours

Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum…

blocks.text: Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

blocks.caption: A visitor takes a picture of the platinum and diamond necklace, which dates from 1939 and belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt, at the Pierres Précieuses exhibition in Paris. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

blocks.caption: Queen Nazli of Egypt, right, wearing the necklace at Princess Fawzia’s wedding in Cairo, 1939. Also pictured, from left, are: Queen Farida, King Farouk, Fawzia and Crown Prince Mohammad. Photograph: Bettmann Archive

blocks.text: The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.
A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.
after newsletter promotion
In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.
This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

articles.title: BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: The BBC's Lucy Williamson reports on settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone.

blocks.text: Violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank is set to reach record levels this year, as human rights groups warn that they are increasingly spreading into new areas of the territory.
Attacks on Palestinians have risen under Israel's current government, alongside a rapid increase in Israeli settlements, illegal under international law.
Many of these attacks are not widely reported on.
The BBC's Lucy Williamson has been tracking settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
articles.summary:
Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard

The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop…

blocks.text: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.

The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
“The stop is ‌a ⁠routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.

Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify ​the vessels or provide a date.

The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. The Navy Times also reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.
On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard told MS Now that her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.

Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which is defined as someone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.

The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.
The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.
The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.
In a statement to the Guardian on Friday, a navy official said “our first responsibility following this incident was the Sailor’s safety and well-being”.
“He was safely recovered, medically evacuated from the ship and evaluated by medical professionals,” they said. “He continues to have access to appropriate care and support.”

They added that “medical care and administrative or disciplinary processes are separate, and one does not preclude the other”, and “the command has the discretion to address misconduct based on the totality of the circumstances”.

“Because this involves an individual Sailor’s protected medical information and an ongoing personnel matter, we cannot discuss the specific evidence, medical care or ongoing proceedings,” the navy added.
The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.
Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.

articles.title: What 'The Odyssey' can teach us about climate chaos
articles.summary: The Bronze Age collapse may have started with a water crisis. Today’s droughts raise the unsettling question of whether it could happen again.

image.caption: Homer's epic, "The Odyssey," is set against a backdrop of civilisational collapseImage: Cinema Publishers Collection/IMAGO

blocks.text: Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster has drawn tens of millions of viewers into a world of stormy seas and cities on fire.
Minus the monsters, that world is based in reality. "The Odyssey" — a post-Trojan War survival story — is set during the Bronze Age collapse of civilization.
A new study links that collapse to a severe climate shift. And the authors warn of "implications for the future."
Scientists have long known about a mysterious and severe drought that struck more than 3,000 years ago, overlapping with the disintegration of kingdoms and states across the Mediterranean.
Ancient Epic: The Odyssey on Film
Research published last month sheds light on the potential cause of that drought: A slow drying trend and a quicker natural cycle of dry weather stacked on top of each other.

By the late Bronze Age, the West African monsoon system had been shrinking for thousands of years, turning a green Sahara into desert. Less rain over Africa meant less over the Mediterranean. That trend amplified when the region hit a dry spell caused by natural climate cycles from the Atlantic, which saw the region swing between decades-long wet and dry periods.
Katherine Power, the Stockholm University scientist who led the study, said the environment at the time could explain the mass migration and conflicts of the Odyssey's era.
For decades, scholars have speculated on the reason for the large-scale movement during this time — which is also referred to as the period of the so-called Sea Peoples.

blocks.caption: A copy of a fresco from the Central Court at Knossos, Greece, one of the palace cities abandoned during the Late Bronze AgeImage: World History Archive/picture alliance

blocks.text: Archeologists argue that climate shifts could help explain the migration and political collapse at the end of the Bronze Age. The new findings add puzzle pieces.
"We don't know necessarily why those people moved," Power said. "But if we can say, 'hey, the climate was getting worse and worse to survive,' that could be a potential reason."
'A perfect storm of calamities'

And that, she says, is relevant to today. Europe's major rivers are at record lows, and drought is creating conditions for devastating wildfires as well as fueling historic crop-loss. That includes France's lowest maize harvest in 50 years.

blocks.caption: Heatwaves and drought have wreaked havoc with cropsImage: Patricia Huchot-Boissier/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: The same cycles of wetting and drying from the Atlantic are still at play, but they're now happening in the context of a world that's heating as a result of humans burning oil, gas and coal.
"I think it is even more alarming and even more of a threat," Power said.
But does what happened then give insights into what might happen now?

Eric H. Cline, archeologist at George Washington University, who wrote a book on the roots of the Bronze Age crisis, said drought and disease were part of the "perfect storm of calamities" that led to societal downfall.
He sees parallels to today. In an email to DW, he said "we should be very concerned" about climate change as a stressor for the collapse of civilization. "That fear is not too dramatic at all."
He added that on his most optimistic days, he believes "we will come to our senses and sidestep that possibility at some point."
How climate change is teaming up with 'Super El Nino'
Was there a trigger moment for the collapse?
Power's research sought to explore what patterns might lie behind isolated Bronze Age drought events.

They started by examining plant spores, ice cores, cave stones, and other natural records that pointed to drought. Then, she and co-author Stockholm paleoclimate scientist Qiong Zhang turned to modeling to get a broader picture.

Their model looked at the whole planet, overlaid with a grid, each cell covering a roughly 125-kilometer (78-mile) area. A supercomputer then calculated the conditions in each of these cells, for every month, across thousands of years. That let the scientists look at the entire Mediterranean.
"We're not now stuck with just one core or one cave," Power said. "We can see farther afield and build a whole picture."

blocks.caption: The ruins of Tiryns, a Greek palace city that declined during the Bronze Age Collapse amid drought and regional upheavalImage: Ian Murray/imageBROKER/IMAGO

blocks.text: What they found was not a single event that dramatically and suddenly changed the climate. Instead, shorter cycles of wetting and drying lined up with a longer warming trend.

"When we are looking for connections between climate changes and civilization changes, we often are looking for that big, huge, abrupt, catastrophic event," Power said, adding that it is "slow, gradual changes that push a society over a threshold.”
She said it could have been a steady fall in water supply that led to a slow decline in crops, which prompted people to migrate, triggering conflict.

"It doesn't take very much to push a society over the threshold that they're comfortable with," Power said. "What if you add something more to the mix? Maybe then that pushes you a bit farther, and you can't quite recover from that."

articles.title: Influential humanists: These are the winners of the Goethe Medal 2026
articles.summary: The prestigious German cultural award recognizes the artistic work and commitment to cultural dialogue of Arvo Pärt, Anita Raja and Prodromos Tsinikoris.

image.caption: Agents of intercultural dialogue: documentary theater director Prodromos Tsinikoris, composer Arvo Pärt and translator Anita RajaImage: DW/picture alliance/Imago

blocks.text: Estonian classical music composer Arvo Pärt, Italian literary translator Anita Raja and Greek theater director and actor Prodromos Tsinikoris are the three recipients of the 2026 Goethe Medal, an annual award that honors international public figures who contribute to creating cultural bridges between Germany and partner countries.
The annual award, presented this year on August 28 in Weimar, is one of the most prestigious awards in Germany for international cultural work.
So what connects these three personalities to Germany's culture?
A prolific German exile: Estonian composer Arvo Pärt

Considered one of the most influential figures in contemporary classical music since the 1960s, the Estonian composer is renowned for his minimalist, contemplative compositional technique called "tintinnabula."
With his iconic works including "Für Alina" (1976), "Fratres" (1977), "Tabula rasa" (1977) and "Spiegel im Spiegel" (1978), Pärt is one of the most performed living composers in the world.

In 1980, the composer was forced to leave his home country, and his works were banned in the Soviet Union. After leaving then Soviet Estonia, Pärt settled in West Berlin with his family. He lived in Germany for nearly three decades.

"Germany plays such an important part in my father's work," Michael Pärt told DW. The composer's son added that his renowned father found creative freedom through his collaborations with different German conductors and musicians. He was also inspired to compose works to German texts.
Goethe Medal 2026 for Arvo Pärt
Pärt's minimalist and spiritual works found a broad audience in the West thanks to the recordings of Manfred Eicher, founder of the Munich-based record label ECM.
After Estonia gained independence in 1991, Pärt reestablished contacts with his home country and returned there permanently in 2010.

The composer, who turned 90 in September 2025, now lives in the Estonian village of Laulasmaa, where the Arvo Pärt Centre opened in 2018. It is directed by his son, Michael Pärt, who will be traveling to Weimar to pick up the award on behalf of his father.
One of the most significant translators from German into Italian: Anita Raja
Born in Naples in 1953 to an Italian father and a German mother, Anita Raja studied literature in Rome, where she still lives.
Specialized in the translation of modern German-language authors, Raja introduced East German author Christa Wolf to Italian readers with her translation of "Cassandra" in the early 1980s.

"Anita Raja's translation is a translation from woman to woman. It's very empathetic, very powerful. It shows that there really was a surprisingly magical connection between the author and the translator," noted renowned Italian actor Sonia Bergamasco at a recent event marking the release of a new edition of the novel.
Wolf became a widely celebrated author in Italy thanks to this first translation, and Raja then went on to translate many more of Wolf's novels.
Goethe Medal 2026 for Anita Raja
She has also translated the works of other major German-language writers, including Georg Büchner, Franz Kafka and Ingeborg Bachmann.

All while translating literature, Raja also worked full-time as a librarian in Rome. She became the founding director of the Biblioteca Europea in Rome in 2005, heading it for more than 10 years. She turned the library into a model project focusing on the promotion of European cultures, languages and international cooperation.
Prodromos Tsinikoris: Documentary theater as a bridge between cultures
Born in the West German city of Wuppertal in 1981 as the son of Greek labor migrants, Prodromos Tsinikoris is one of the leading voices in contemporary Greek and European theater.
As a theater director, actor and dramaturg, he creates documentary productions exploring the themes of migration, social inequality and historical perspectives.
Goethe Medal 2026 for Prodromos Tsinikoris
His audio walk "In the middle of the street" centers on homeless people during Greece's financial crisis.

The documentary theater production "Clean City," co-created with Anestis Azas, focuses on the lives of migrant cleaners, juxtaposing their personal testimonies with the rhetoric of neo-fascist movements who want to "clean" Greece of its foreigners and refugees.
In the play "96%" Tsinikoris deals with the Holocaust of the Jews of Thessaloniki and the looting of their property during the Nazi occupation.

From 2015 to 2020, Tsinikoris directed the Experimental Stage at the National Theater in Athens. Today, he is co-curator of the International Forest Festival in Thessaloniki and teaches at the National Theater's directing school in Athens.

Many of Tsinikoris' plays have been developed and presented in Germany. His work has also circulated broadly across Europe, particularly through documentary theater festivals and major public theaters.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.summary: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.caption: Sludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.
after newsletter promotion

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Why Germany's military is betting on gamers
articles.summary: For the past 10 years, the German armed forces — the Bundeswehr — have been represented at Gamescom, Cologne's video game trade fair. They've been criticized for trying to draw more young people into…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr will once again be represented at the Gamescom video game trade fair in Cologne in 2026Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show.

Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks.

Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation.
Career advice in camouflage
The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since.

A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities.
Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking.

blocks.caption: The Caracal off-road vehicle is a popular photo opportunity at the Bundeswehr boothImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength.

New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games.
Do gamers make good soldiers?

A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people found it likely that video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier.

blocks.caption: Lieutenant General Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel ManagementImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do."

For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian."
Criticism of Bundeswehr presence
The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV.

Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall.

blocks.caption: 'Level Up for Your Career': Peace activists criticize the Bundeswehr's use of gaming jargonImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch says the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service.

"We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW.
For two days, the peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls, providing information about conscientious objection to military service.
Bundeswehr: Not just any job
"Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement.
Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people."

He reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," Sieger said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years."
What do young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence?

"Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’
articles.summary: Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley council

blocks.text: A Sydney library has returned to its borrowing shelves a book critical of Israel called How to Sell a Genocide following a public campaign and an intervention from the State Library of New South Wales.
Waverley library removed the book “for review” earlier this month after the Jewish news outlet JWire reported it had approached the council.

JWire said a survivor of December’s antisemitic attack at Bondi, during which 15 people were killed, saw How to Sell a Genocide on the “new release / hot item” shelf and wrote on Facebook that the display was distressing for survivors and bereaved families.
Guardian Australia was unable to locate the Facebook post. Waverley library at Bondi Junction is in the same council area as Bondi beach.
A staff member at the council-operated library on Friday confirmed the book was back on its shelves. Waverley council was contacted for comment.

The State Library had written to the council reminding it of its obligations under guidelines issued by the Library Council of NSW and the Library Act “which was amended in 2026 to reinforce their independence to develop and maintain collections”.
“The State Library of NSW supports free and equitable access to information,” a spokesperson said.

“The library acknowledges that some books and materials may not align with everyone’s personal views, experiences or beliefs, but supports the right of individuals to make their own choices about what they read, view and access.
“The library has outlined to Waverley council the law and policy relevant to this situation.”

Ramia Abdo Sultan, a lawyer, helped organise a change.org petition calling for the book to be returned to the shelves. She said in a social media post on Thursday that Waverley library’s manager had notified staff that was happening.
“There are 21 people so far queued up in a waiting list for that book,” Abdo Sultan, a board member of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, said.
The petition to restore the book was signed by almost 2,500 people.
“We acknowledge and respect the grief and trauma experienced by victims of violence and antisemitism,” it stated.

“However, individual distress, offence or political disagreement should not determine what the broader public is permitted to access through a public library. Readers should be afforded the opportunity to access books freely and form their own opinions on the contents of the book.”
The book, published by Pluto Press and written by Adam Johnson, critiques what it claims is the US media’s “complicity in the destruction of Gaza”.

Johnson welcomed the decision to reinstate his book but criticised the council for “thus far refusing to answer what complaint prompted the book’s removal”. Johnson said he hoped to find out “through legal channels”.
“It’s obviously a good development the council decided to end their ban of the book amid pressure from free speech and Palestine activists, whose support I am grateful for,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“But it was never about one library or one book, but about the increased suppression of pro-Palestine speech in Australia, which has radically escalated over the past seven months. Attempts to blame Palestine solidarity and sympathies for the Bondi attack, as the book ban advocates repeatedly did, is the real story. This false and sleazy conflation must stop.”
Guardian Australia approached the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (Ecaj) and the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies for comment.
Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive officer of Ecaj, previously welcomed the book’s removal.
“A book of this sort has no place on the shelves of a library, especially one within minutes of where Australians were slaughtered [at Bondi],” Ryvchin told the Sydney Morning Herald.
“I commend the individual who spotted the book, herself a survivor of the massacre, and acted to have it removed.”
Bart Shteinman, an executive member of the progressive Jewish Council of Australia, said the book should “never have been removed in the first place”.

“This debacle should be a lesson for other councils that stifling literary freedom only confuses and undermines the critical struggle against antisemitism and all forms of racism,” he said on Thursday.
“Banning books is not something any council should be doing.”

The president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, Nasser Mashni, said: “That a single complaint was enough to trigger the removal of a book about the genocide in Palestine should concern every Australian who values free inquiry and open debate. These efforts must be resisted.”

Multiple human rights groups have said Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, which Israel denies. In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry found Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

At the time the book was removed, a Waverley council spokesperson said: “The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection.”

articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
articles.summary:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor…

blocks.text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.
Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

blocks.caption: Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”
It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Protests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya. Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”
The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.
That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
articles.summary:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release…

blocks.text: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.
Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.
Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.
The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.
Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’
articles.summary:
President denies visit was to gain support for Iran sanctions or due to fears that Putin plans to ‘test Nato resolve’

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by the Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.

Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.
“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.
“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.

“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.

The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year. Trump’s efforts to end the war – which he once vowed to bring to a conclusion on “day one” of his second presidency – have proven unsuccessful, despite his friendly personal relations with Putin.
Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin during his visit.
after newsletter promotion

Washington and Moscow have found themselves on opposite sides following Trump’s decision last February to go to war with Iran, with Russian satellite technology said to have been used to help Iranian forces with precise targeting of US and allied bases in the Gulf and beyond.

With military hostilities at an impasse, the US treasury department this week unveiled a new program of economic warfare against the Tehran regime involving secondary sanctions against countries that trade with it. To be effective, it would need the cooperation of allies of Iran such as Russia and China, experts say.
Peskov did not give a reason for Ratcliffe’s visit, but described forecasts that it would lead to an upturn in US-Russian relations as “premature”, the Washington Post reported.

“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive phenomenon, a positive process. These contacts often continue even in the most difficult moments of bilateral relations,” Peskov told reporters. “But whether this will affect, on the whole, the process of bringing our bilateral relations out of the deep crisis they are in – it’s premature to say at this point.”
In recent days, Ukraine has targeted Russia’s energy infrastructure and online retail facilities in long-distance strikes, while Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Kyiv.

articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
articles.summary:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents…

blocks.text: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment

blocks.text: The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive
articles.summary:
Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost

As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza, and Julian Borger

blocks.text: As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.

With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.

Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.

“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.

blocks.caption: Yousef at work in 2024. He was killed by a drone-fired missile that year aged 24. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”

Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.
The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.

Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.
“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee works on his plants nursery in Gaza

blocks.text: Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.

He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.

“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.”

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee checks the state of crops grown for the production of seeds. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Increased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, but according to UN agencies there are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse.

Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production.
“Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee harvesting aubergines. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Based on satellite data, the FAO estimates that little more than a quarter of Gaza’s total prewar cropland, 4,100 hectares, remains accessible, and only about 3%, 450 hectares, is undamaged, free of debris and ready for immediate cultivation.
Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army has pushed the “yellow line” steadily forward over the course of the ceasefire.

Using specialised satellite imagery, the human rights advocacy group Forensic Architecture carried out a survey of flora across Gaza as a measurable proxy for cultivable land. It found that nearly 68% of the territory’s flora was on the Israeli side of the yellow line and another 5% was inside a buffer zone declared by the army, delineated on maps with an orange line, where it is extremely dangerous for Palestinians to venture.

Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, was shot dead along with another man when they came within range of Israeli sniper positions. Their bodies were left out in the open for two days because it was too dangerous for their relatives to retrieve them.

The family’s old farm is now under Israeli control, so after the ceasefire was declared they came to Beit Lahiya to try to start again from scratch on leased land. Since last October the army has pushed the yellow line forward, swallowing up nearby farms in west Beit Lahiya.

“The expansion has had a devastating impact on the agricultural sector,” Abu Rabee said. “Fertile farmland that farmers had worked tirelessly to cultivate after spending everything they had or even borrowing money, simply it was seized just as it was ready for harvest, leaving them with nothing.”

blocks.caption: Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, who was shot dead in July. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: On the remaining land, the challenges appear endless. With hardly any livestock left, there is little homegrown dung-based fertiliser, so the family are improvising by piling decaying vegetation under tarpaulins. Meanwhile, they are battling nematodes and other soil infestations and a chronic lack of water, all the time under the constant, unpredictable threat of death.

Abu Rabee said: “Stray bullets frequently reach this area and strike many places around us. Many people have also been wounded in the streets as a result of indiscriminate attacks. I fear for my own life simply because I’m a farmer.”

articles.title: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost

image.caption: B.C.'s forestry industry is expected to be one of the hardest-hit sectors by the Trump administration's new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods. Most wood and forest products exported by B.C. are sold to the U.S., valued at about $6.7 billion by the provincial government in 2024. (Justin Tang/The

blocks.text: With the Trump administration's promise to impose more tariffs on us in January, many Canadians are asking: What leverage should we use to get them to change course?

The question suggests that there are actually real things we can do to change U.S. President Donald Trump's mind — that if Canada hits back hard enough, or demonstrates its willingness to suffer enough, we will get that policy change.

Christopher Ragan, the founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy and former chair of Canada’s Ecofiscal Commission put it this way: "Canada is in a set of negotiations with a party that appears to be unpredictable, volatile, so I don't think anybody really knows what's going to work here."
Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, said if Canadians are willing to suffer the consequences, there are plenty of ways to punch back at the U.S.
Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’

"You first strike the things they've said are the most important to them," Drummond said. "They made it painfully clear that the only thing they want or need from Canada is oil, and maybe for a while electricity.
"We've had an export tax on oil and natural gas before and we could introduce that. We could also introduce quotas," he said.

Canada's leverage is significant when it comes to energy and fertilizer. In 2025 Canadian comodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81.3 per cent of imported electricity, almost 100 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.
A number of non-tariff options

And while there's still a long way to go before Canada fully develops its critical mineral reserves, Drummond says we could notify the U.S. that they won't get preferential access when those reserves come online.
"We could also restrict American access to Canada," Drummond said. "In the extreme we could require a visa and we could be very stingy with them."
Canada could also refuse to buy the F-35 fighter jets from the U.S. and choose instead to go with the Gripen from Sweden, he said.
Canadian banks, governments, pension funds and others currently hold about $459.6 billion US in U.S. treasury bonds.

"Given that the U.S. is tormented at the moment trying to get their long-term bond yields down, if we said we were going to divest ourselves of those, or at least not buy any more, that would tick them off," Drummond said.

items: Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'
Carney says he'll resume negotiating when Trump team has the 'right attitude'

blocks.text: Drummond also said that Canada's CPP fund could divest itself of all U.S. assets (51 per cent of the $864-billion fund is invested in the U.S., compared to just 12 per cent in Canada), but that would open the door to using Canadians' retirement as a political tool and placing retirees at risk — a step he said the country should avoid taking.
"You could put back the digital services tax, for example. Why the hell did we give it away? We got absolutely nothing for giving it away," Drummond said.
He says we could also eliminate the Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit, which he says results in lost tax revenue of about $500 million annually, with little economic benefit for Canada.
"So it could be fairly broad-based, it could be export restrictions or export taxes, it could be any number of things," Drummond said.
Some economists warn that while employing these non-tariff measures might feel good and would certainly harm the U.S. economy, they would hurt Canada's economy more.
Long-term, short-term pain

"I think emotions are pretty high and there's just a desire to lash out, but cooler heads require us to take a moment to think about what it is we're trying to achieve," said Trevor Tombe, director of fiscal and economic policy at the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy.

Tombe says the 50 per cent tariffs on about $27 billion of Canadian goods represent a hit to Canadian GDP of about 0.4 or 0.5 per cent, and taking retaliatory action that costs Canada more than that doesn't make economic sense unless it changes U.S. behaviour.

"That's a lot easier said than done," Tombe said. "And if we do things that increase costs in the United States, that might very well play into the hands of the U.S. administration by allowing them to blame Canada."
Beyond hurting Canada's economy in the short term, there's another negative side effect: hurting it in the long term.
Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney

"Maybe we have a lot of leverage, a lot of ability to impose pain, but it comes at a huge cost for us because we are both losing revenue and we are potentially severing relationships with our best customer," said Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa.
What if, for example, the U.S. replaced all Canadian oil with Venezuelan oil in a decade?

By way of example, Alschner says, China's export controls on critical minerals have prompted the U.S. to try to strike new deals, find new customers and build new critical mineral supply chains. Perhaps the best example of this is Canada's push to diversify in the face of the Trump administration's trade war.

"Even if you do it for a short period of time, you're sending a signal that this can be turned on and off. And so maybe the United States will not have time to mitigate that particular disruption at that moment, but it will then put measures in place to mitigate it in the future," he said.
Alschner also said bringing back concessions such as reimposing the Digital Services Tax or cancelling tax credits would be a direct provocation with an unclear dividend.
Sometimes there is only the fight

Ragan from McGill University says the U.S. would likely react strongly to export controls or taxes that drive up U.S. gas prices. That would risk turning energy scarcity caused by Canada into something that unites Americans against this country.

"That move escalates the trade war a few notches at once," Ragan said. "I say this half jokingly, but I wonder if you restricted electricity sales or oil sales or natural gas sales, whether that would lead Donald Trump to calling the troops. I'm not so sure."

Some economists say that rather than take actions that cost the Canadian economy in the short and long term, Canada should focus on how it can make up the difference with trade expansion and diversification abroad while building at home.
"Another way to think about the U.S. right now that I find kind of helpful is that they are flailing around in increasingly irrational ways and we are getting hit in the face," Tombe said.

"To the extent that their moves are crazy and not grounded in economic rationale, the best option might be to step back, try to weather the storm, and hopefully they work out their own issues domestically."

items: Interprovincial trade barriers are falling. But rewriting old rules will take time
Will auto tariffs be a permanent roadblock for a Canada-U.S. trade deal?

blocks.text: Tombe says that aside from the broader move to diversify our exports, sign new trade deals and build at home, Canada still hasn't liberalized internal trade, an opportunity he calls low-hanging fruit.
He says that by simply recognizing credentials across the country, Canada could boost productivity enough to offset a 25 per cent across-the-board tariff.

Alschner says the advantage Canada has right now is that the EU and other global trading partners are locked in similar trade disputes with the United States, which means they may be highly motivated to work with Canada.

"We should really use this as an opportunity to forcibly substitute U.S. imports with strategically selected non-U.S. imports," Alschner said. "We should say to the European Union, 'All right, what are the things that you can sell to us that the United States used to sell to us?'"
Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs
Tombe notes that while there are plenty of economic reasons to avoid employing non-tariff retaliatory measures in this trade fight, Canada's battle with the U.S. isn't entirely economic.
The U.S., as Prime Minister Mark Carney has said, wants to break us so it can own us, and some say a threat to our sovereignty requires an un-economic response.
"I'm getting a little tired, mainly, with fellow economists who point out that it's harmful to Canada to retaliate. I think that's pretty narrow-minded," Drummond said.

"I'd like to give that advice to the kid in the schoolyard who's getting bullied, [because] it's not much more complicated than that: If you want to stop a bully you have to be prepared to get your nose bloodied. It just eggs them on otherwise."
